name: Treating acid reflux for voice

lead: People with chronic hoarseness or frequent throat clearing are sometimes evaluated for laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR, or silent reflux) and treat it to get a clearer voice.

LPR is the backward flow of stomach contents into the throat, thought to irritate the larynx and cause hoarseness and strain. Many patients have little or no heartburn. Trials of acid-suppressing drugs for LPR have shown mixed results, and the diagnosis itself is debated.

paras: Management commonly combines diet and lifestyle changes, medication such as proton-pump inhibitors, alginate products, and sometimes surgery, usually guided by a clinician.
Hoarseness has many causes, and clinicians generally recommend evaluation when it persists. PPIs have their own adverse-effect profiles, and long-term use warrants clinician involvement.

angle.text: Controlling reflux reduces irritation of the larynx, which can ease hoarseness and give a clearer voice. Treatment studies for LPR are mixed and the diagnosis is debated.

lead: Treating acid reflux for voice refers to managing laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR), sometimes called silent reflux, with the aim of relieving hoarseness and throat clearing and getting a clearer, steadier voice. LPR is the backward flow of stomach contents into the larynx, oropharynx or nasopharynx.[1]

Hoarseness is considered a primary symptom of LPR and can lead to vocal strain and fatigue, and may progress to muscle tension dysphonia that can persist after reflux is controlled.[1] Many patients have little or no heartburn.[1] For people who care about how their voice sounds, controlling reflux is a way to remove an irritant that may be roughening it.

Management commonly combines lifestyle measures, proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) and alginate products.[1] Controlled studies of PPIs for LPR have given mixed results, and the diagnosis itself is debated.[1][2][3]

paras: LPR is often treated as a subtype of GERD but is described as having a different pathophysiology and symptom profile. Throat clearing occurs in about 87% of LPR cases compared with fewer than 5% of GERD cases, while heartburn appears in about 20% versus over 80%.[1]

Symptoms are nonspecific, and laryngoscopic findings such as redness and swelling have been found in many people without symptoms. Questionnaires such as the Reflux Symptom Index, laryngoscopy and pH monitoring are used.[1] A blinded study in which five otolaryngologists rated 120 laryngoscopy video segments found poor agreement on reflux-related findings, and its authors described the laryngoscopic diagnosis as highly subjective.[4]

Lifestyle measures listed include avoiding chocolate, caffeine, acidic and fatty foods, weight loss, quitting smoking, limiting alcohol, and not eating shortly before bed. PPIs are the most common medication, alginates form a foam barrier, and fundoplication surgery may be offered when medical management fails.[1]

Vocal-hygiene programs address reflux alongside allergies as non-speech factors affecting the voice, and voice therapy from a speech-language pathologist may be needed for persistent strain.[5][1] Reinke's edema is another voice condition for which reflux control is part of first-line management.[6]

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of omeprazole for two months in 30 patients with pH-confirmed reflux laryngitis found greater improvement than placebo in hoarseness (when baseline hoarseness was mild) and throat clearing. Other symptoms improved in both groups, and endoscopic signs did not change significantly.[2] A systematic review of PPI treatment for LPR found benefit in uncontrolled studies but no significant difference from placebo in six randomized trials.[3] Wikipedia likewise cites a 2006 esomeprazole trial with a disappointing response and a 2008 review finding many studies in which PPIs were no more effective than placebo.[1]

A 2017 meta-analysis found alginate therapy effective for GERD symptoms, and a review covered voice outcomes in 1,483 patients.[1] Separately, a randomized trial of voice therapy in 204 people with hoarseness lasting at least two months found improved voice quality at six weeks by patient and observer ratings; that trial did not focus on reflux.[7]

timeline.event: Placebo-controlled trial of omeprazole in pH-confirmed reflux laryngitis reports improved hoarseness and throat clearing.[2]
Systematic review finds randomized trials show no significant PPI benefit over placebo for empiric LPR treatment.[3]
